title: Widening gap between rich and poor

samples.text:
In many countries, the difference between rich people and poor people is becoming bigger and bigger. In my opinion, this is a clearly negative development, because it causes many problems for poor people and also for the whole society.

Firstly, when the gap is big, poor people have less opportunities in their life. Rich families can pay for private schools, extra classes and good universities for their children, but poor families cannot afford this. As a result, children from poor family often get lower-paid jobs when they grow up, and they stay poor. This is not fair, because talented children should have the same chance to succeed.

Secondly, a big gap between rich and poor can cause social problems. When people see that some people have very expensive cars and houses but they cannot even pay their rent, they feel angry and unhappy. This can lead to more crime and less trust in the government. In some cities, rich and poor people live in completely different areas and they never meet each other, so the society become divided.

Some people say that inequality is not a problem because it motivate people to work harder and become rich. It is true that people need some rewards for hard work, but when the gap is too big, poor people feel that working hard is useless because they can never catch up.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that the growing gap between the richest and poorest people is a negative development. Governments should try to reduce it, for example by giving free education and making rich people pay more tax.
samples.why: Clear negative position · relevant main ideas and a counter-argument, though development is general · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary with repetition (rich, poor) · several agreement and quantifier errors.

samples.text:
In many nations, the wealth and income of the richest citizens have grown far faster than those of the poorest, causing the gap between them to widen. I believe this is a highly negative development, as it limits opportunity and threatens social stability.

The first problem is that growing inequality reduces social mobility. Wealthy families can invest heavily in their children's education, health and connections, while low-income families often struggle to meet basic needs. As a result, a child's future increasingly depends on the family they are born into rather than on their talent or effort. This is not only unfair to individuals but also wasteful for society, since the abilities of many capable young people are never fully developed.

Secondly, a large gap between rich and poor can damage the cohesion of a society. When people feel that the economic system benefits only a small elite, they tend to lose trust in institutions and politicians. This frustration can fuel social unrest and support for extreme political movements. In addition, the wealthy are able to exert disproportionate influence over political decisions, for example through lobbying, which may lead to policies that further protect their interests.

Some argue that inequality is a natural result of a free economy and that it encourages people to work hard and take risks. There is some truth in this, as a certain degree of difference in income rewards effort and skill. However, when the gap becomes extreme, it no longer act as a motivation, because the poorest see no realistic way of improving their situation.

In conclusion, although some inequality is inevitable, a continually growing gap between the richest and the poorest is harmful. It restricts opportunities, weakens trust and concentrates power, and governments should therefore take steps to reduce it.
samples.why: Clear, consistent negative position · ideas extended and supported, counter-argument rebutted · well-organised paragraphs with a range of linkers · good vocabulary (social mobility, lobbying) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
In a large number of countries, the share of national wealth held by the most affluent has grown while the incomes of those at the bottom have stagnated. Some economists regard this as a tolerable by-product of growth, but I consider the widening gap to be an unmistakably negative development.

The most fundamental objection concerns opportunity. When wealth is heavily concentrated, advantage becomes self-perpetuating: affluent families can secure better schooling, healthcare and professional networks for their children, while those on low incomes struggle to meet everyday costs. Over successive generations, life chances come to depend increasingly on birth rather than merit, and a society squanders the potential of countless able people who never have the means to develop it.

A second objection is political. Extreme economic disparities tend to translate into disparities of influence, since those with vast resources can fund campaigns, shape public debate and lobby for favourable treatment. The result is a system that responds more readily to the concerns of the few than to those of the many. Unsurprisingly, citizens who perceive the system as rigged become disillusioned with mainstream institutions, and this erosion of trust can open the door to polarisation and instability.

Defenders of inequality argue that the prospect of great rewards drives enterprise and innovation. This argument has some force when applied to moderate differences in income, which do reflect variations in skill and effort. It becomes far less convincing, however, when the gap grows so wide that those at the bottom have no realistic prospect of advancement, for at that point inequality ceases to motivate and instead breeds resignation.

In conclusion, while a degree of inequality is an inevitable feature of any market economy, its continued growth undermines equal opportunity, distorts democratic politics and weakens social cohesion. It is therefore a development that governments should actively work to reverse.
samples.why: Forceful, fully developed negative judgement · counter-argument evaluated with precision · logical, well-signposted progression · wide, sophisticated vocabulary (self-perpetuating, squanders) · complex structures used flexibly and accurately.
